Taraazu Commerce Systems: Four Hundred Coins and a Menu Nobody Priced

Ahmedabad, Sunday night, 11 October 2026

The night before

The building on Prahlad Nagar Road was empty except for the security guard and the hum of a server closet nobody had decommissioned after the move to the cloud. Meghna Trivedi, vice-president of product at Taraazu Commerce Systems, had come in at eight on a Sunday evening because at home her daughter's Navratri garba practice made thinking impossible, and because at nine the next morning she had to walk into the leadership review and lock the engineering roadmap for the Diwali-to-March window. On Friday the same roadmap went to the board.

Across two monitors were three rankings of the same nine features. The first was the outcome of the buy-a-feature workshop she had designed and run in August, in which twenty-four of Taraazu's distributor customers had spent play money on a priced menu. The second was that same spending re-tallied by the company's data scientist in Toronto, weighted by what each customer actually paid Taraazu every year, and it put a different feature on top. The third came from three hundred and ten kirana retailers who had done a version of the exercise inside the retailer app, and it was very nearly the first ranking upside down. Beside them sat a re-estimate memo from engineering, dated 22 September, which said the item distributors had funded most enthusiastically would cost not ₹180 lakh but something closer to ₹340 lakh, and that four others had not been re-estimated at all.

Meghna had run the workshop precisely so that this meeting would not come down to whoever spoke last and loudest. What she had instead was a result that could be read four ways, a capacity number that made most of the debate academic, and a growing suspicion that the most important item was one she had never put on the menu.

Taraazu Commerce Systems

Taraazu was founded in Ahmedabad in 2018 by Sandeep Iyer, who had grown up in his family's Coimbatore distribution business, and Farida Qureshi, an engineer who had spent nine years building warehouse systems in Bengaluru. Their observation was ordinary and correct: India's consumer goods reach roughly 1.3 crore kirana stores through a layer of mid-sized distributors who ran on Tally, WhatsApp and paper challans, and whose single largest source of working-capital pain was the months-long lag between running a principal's trade scheme and being reimbursed for it. Taraazu built the distributor's operating system — order capture, stock, scheme and claim settlement, credit, and a retailer-facing ordering app — and sold it as software, at first for ₹8,000 a month.

By September 2026 the company served 1,900 distributor businesses across twenty states, carried about 4.1 lakh retailers on the retailer app, and had ₹67 crore of annual recurring revenue growing at 38 per cent, with a further 28 per cent of revenue from usage-based payment and credit fees the finance team had never attributed cleanly to accounts. Engineering sat in Bengaluru and Pune; design was led from Berlin, data science from Toronto, Gulf and South-East Asian customer success from Singapore; and a small enterprise sales effort ran out of New Jersey, selling to Indian-origin distribution houses.

One early decision shaped everything available to Meghna in 2026. In 2020, racing to win a marquee account that distributed a single large food principal, the founders hard-coded a one-distributor-one-principal assumption into the ledger and the scheme engine. It was right at the time: it let them ship claim settlement in eleven weeks and add three hundred customers in eighteen months. But by 2026, 62 per cent of Taraazu's distributors carried four principals or more, and every feature that had to reason across principals — consolidated schemes, cross-principal credit exposure, a single stock view — hit that assumption and cost two to three times what an outsider would guess. Vikram Sahni, who led the Pune platform pod, had been asking for a ledger refactor for five quarters. It had never reached a roadmap, because it was not a feature and no customer had ever asked for it by name.

A second constraint arrived in December 2024, when the New Jersey office closed a three-year, ₹4.2 crore-a-year contract with Shireen Foods Trading FZE, a Dubai-based, Indian-origin distributor supplying Gulf retail. It committed Taraazu to Gulf VAT handling, multi-currency settlement and a right-to-left Arabic interface by 31 December 2026, with ₹35 lakh of service credits if it slipped. That work consumed roughly ₹60 lakh of build capacity and never appeared on the buy-a-feature menu, because it was not a choice.

Figure A. Two commitments — the 2020 ledger shortcut and the 2024 Gulf contract — were settled long before the August workshop, and neither appeared on the menu customers were asked to spend against.

The industry

Taraazu operated in a market being rebuilt underneath it. On one flank were the well-capitalised business-to-business commerce platforms — Udaan, ElasticRun, Jumbotail — which did not sell software to distributors so much as attempt to replace parts of the distribution layer, and Reliance Retail's JioMart Partner programme, which reached kiranas at a price no software vendor could match. On the other flank sat the sales-force-automation vendors — Bizom, FieldAssist, Botree — whose relationships ran to the consumer-goods principals such as Dabur, Britannia, Parle and Amul rather than to the distributors, and whose products therefore optimised for what a principal wanted to see. Underneath everybody lay Tally, still the system of record in most back offices.

Regulation kept moving. GST e-invoicing thresholds had ratcheted down year by year, pulling ever-smaller distributors into mandatory electronic invoicing and e-way bills. The Reserve Bank of India's digital lending guidelines had made Taraazu's embedded retailer credit product — where a kirana bought stock on a short line funded by a partner NBFC — much harder to operate without a licensed partner carrying the loss. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act had turned the retailer transaction data Taraazu held into a consent problem, particularly when principals asked for store-level visibility. ONDC offered a distributor-as-seller-node possibility and had so far generated more conference panels than orders. UPI, through NPCI, had become the default settlement rail between retailer and distributor, which was why Taraazu's usage revenue existed at all.

The two-sidedness of the business mattered more than the org chart admitted. Distributors paid Taraazu. Retailers used Taraazu. Principals influenced Taraazu without buying it. Figure B sketches the flows.

Figure B. Only one of the four parties in the picture holds a Taraazu contract. The August workshop gave coins to that party alone.

What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

It began in February 2026, when Tijori Growth Capital signed a ₹95 crore term sheet at a valuation that assumed disciplined execution, and its partner told Sandeep in diligence that the roadmap read like a list of what the loudest three customers had asked for last quarter. Meghna, who had thought the same for a year, proposed a buy-a-feature exercise for the winter release.

In May, Farida's team costed nine candidate features and converted each into workshop coins at a published rate of five coins to ₹1 lakh of build cost, so that a price signalled real effort. The menu totalled ₹880 lakh, or 4,400 coins (Exhibit 1). On 7 August, on the sidelines of a trade-body meeting in Ahmedabad, twenty-four distributor owners — chosen by customer success as engaged, representative and willing to travel — each received a hundred coins. The pool came to 2,400, a little over half the menu, and no customer could buy any item alone. Groups formed at tables, argued in Gujarati and Hindi, and spent (Exhibit 2).

The result looked clean. Multi-principal scheme and claim settlement drew 980 coins against a 900-coin price, funded by nineteen of twenty-four customers — a broad coalition, not one large account's block. Van-sales and route optimisation cleared by twenty coins. Real-time stock visibility for principals also cleared by twenty, but on the strength of six customers, all large. Everything else fell short, including two items the company treated as strategic: the ONDC seller node attracted forty coins, and embedded retailer credit — which Rohan Malhotra's sales team called the number one customer ask in every quarterly review — attracted a hundred and fifty against a price of seven hundred and fifty.

Four things then went wrong, in the order in which they were discovered.

First, at the chief revenue officer's request, Nikhil Varma in Toronto re-tallied the same spending weighted by each distributor's annual revenue to Taraazu, producing Exhibit 4, in which stock visibility rose to first place and van-sales fell behind GST e-invoicing. The six firms that funded stock visibility averaged ₹46 lakh of ARR each; the nineteen behind multi-principal settlement averaged ₹19 lakh. Nothing in the raw data changed. Only the question did.

Second, Lena Brandt's team in Berlin had run a simplified version inside the retailer app between 18 and 29 August: three hundred and ten kirana owners, fifty coins each, the same items at proportionally identical prices. The retailer ranking (Exhibit 3) was almost the inverse of the distributor ranking. WhatsApp order capture, which distributors had funded with five coins out of 2,400, took the largest share of retailer spending; multi-principal settlement took two per cent.

Third, on 22 September, engineering returned re-estimates (Exhibit 5). Multi-principal settlement, bought at ₹180 lakh, was now ₹340 lakh with low confidence, because it could not be built without touching the 2020 ledger. Stock visibility had become cheaper at ₹58 lakh, since much of the reporting work was already being done for Shireen Foods. GST e-invoicing had ceased to be a choice: the threshold change made it mandatory, so it left the discretionary list and took ₹70 lakh of capacity with it. Four items had not been re-estimated at all.

Fourth, and least discussed, Rohan's team had been asking a willingness-to-pay question on renewal calls since July (Exhibit 6). Only four of thirty-one distributors said they would pay more for multi-principal settlement. Eleven would accept a ₹1.50 per-order fee on retailer orders placed through WhatsApp — a feature that drew five coins from distributors and the largest single share from retailers, and which at current volumes would be worth roughly ₹3.1 crore a year.

The people

Meghna Trivedi — VP Product, Ahmedabad
She designed the workshop and owns Monday's lock. Her position is that the exercise must be honoured in some recognisable form or the company will never run one again. Her incentive is credibility: she spent political capital arguing that customers, not executives, should set the ranking. She is not saying that she chose the nine menu items herself, in an afternoon in May, from the existing backlog, and that the ledger refactor and the Gulf commitment were left off because they were not things a customer would recognise.
Sandeep Iyer — co-founder and CEO, Ahmedabad
He wants a roadmap he can defend to Tijori on Friday as evidence of discipline, and publicly backs the workshop result. His incentive is the next tranche, conditional on net revenue retention reaching 118 per cent. He is not saying that he has already told Tijori's partner, informally, that multi-principal settlement is the winter's headline feature.
Farida Qureshi — co-founder and engineering director, Bengaluru
She holds the capacity number: ₹300 lakh of build for October to March, of which ₹160 lakh is spoken for by the Gulf contract, mandatory GST work and platform maintenance, leaving ₹140 lakh discretionary. She argues that a price a customer paid in August cannot bind engineering in October. She is not saying that two senior engineers in the Pune pod have resigned with effect from November, or that her own May estimates excluded QA effort while Pune's re-estimates include it.
Vikram Sahni — platform lead, Pune
He wants the ledger refactor funded now, arguing that three of the nine menu items are expensive only because of the 2020 shortcut and that the workshop prices were therefore fiction. His incentive is technical and personal: he has been overruled five times. He is not saying that two engineers have been on a refactor spike since July, outside any approved plan.
Lena Brandt — principal designer, Berlin
She argues the retailer exercise is the more important signal, because retailer adoption drives the order volume on which Taraazu's usage revenue and its defence against Udaan and JioMart Partner both depend. Her incentive is a research programme she has tried to fund for a year. She is not emphasising that her sample came through an in-app banner and so reached only regular app users, that 41 per cent were in Maharashtra and Gujarat, and that the exercise ran only in Hindi and English.
Nikhil Varma — data scientist, Toronto
He built both tallies and is uncomfortable with how Exhibit 4 is being used. He points out that the ARR weighting was specified after the results were seen, and that it excludes the 28 per cent of revenue that is usage-based — revenue flowing from retailer order volume, not distributor licences. He is not saying he believes the correct weighting is by retailer volume, because he cannot compute it before Monday.
Sharmila Nair — customer-success lead, Singapore
She owns the Shireen Foods relationship and the Gulf deadline, and holds that nothing may be taken from the Gulf allocation. Her incentive is a renewal worth ₹4.2 crore a year and a service-credit clause. She is not saying that Shireen's group finance director asked in September whether Taraazu could also handle their Saudi entity, an expansion nobody has scoped.
Rohan Malhotra — head of enterprise sales, New Jersey
He treats the workshop as an interesting exercise that cannot override pipeline. He wants embedded retailer credit built, because it is what prospects ask about and what differentiates against the incumbents. His incentive is commission weighted to new logos. He is not saying that the product's economics under the RBI's digital lending guidelines require an NBFC partner Taraazu has not signed, and that legal has not returned the review that would let engineering even estimate the work.

Voices

"Nineteen of twenty-four bought it. Not the biggest nineteen — the nineteen. That is the cleanest signal this company has ever had about anything, and we are about to talk ourselves out of it because an estimate moved." Meghna Trivedi, leadership sync, 29 September 2026
"An estimate did not move. We discovered the price was wrong. If a shop advertises a saree at ₹900 and then finds the cloth costs ₹3,400, the customer's decision to buy at ₹900 does not tell you anything about their decision at ₹3,400." Farida Qureshi, same meeting
"Three of your nine items are expensive for exactly one reason and it is a decision we made in 2020. Nobody was allowed to buy that fix in August because it was not on the menu. So the menu priced the symptoms and hid the disease." Vikram Sahni, internal chat thread, 23 September

It says that retailers who already like the app want the app to do more of what they already do on WhatsApp. It cannot tell you anything about the retailers who never opened it, and those are the ones Udaan and JioMart are talking to." Lena Brandt, design review note, 2 October (her own caveat, circulated with the deck)
"Weighting by ARR was my idea and I want to record that I think it is the wrong weight. Our fastest-growing revenue line is per-transaction, and per-transaction revenue comes from retailers placing orders, not from distributors holding licences. We are weighting by the revenue we understand rather than the revenue we are growing." Nikhil Varma, email to Meghna and Sandeep, 5 October

"Anything we take from the Gulf allocation is a ₹35 lakh credit and a conversation I am not going to have in January. Also, they have asked about Saudi. I have not put that anywhere because there is nowhere to put it." Sharmila Nair, Singapore, weekly note, 6 October

The options as Meghna sees them

By Sunday night she had written four on a sheet of paper.

One: honour the workshop

Fund multi-principal settlement, the item nineteen of twenty-four customers bought, and accept that at ₹340 lakh it consumes the discretionary budget two and a half times over. That means either slipping the Gulf work, which Sharmila will not accept, or a difficult conversation about the tranche, or building a thinner version that avoids the ledger and therefore does not do what the nineteen thought they were buying.

Two: follow the revenue

Fund stock visibility at ₹58 lakh and van-sales at ₹96 lakh — ₹154 lakh, marginally over budget — on the strength of Exhibit 4, telling the nineteen that their item comes next release. Cheap, and defensible on Friday. It also means the workshop's winner loses to a weighting devised after the results were known, and that Taraazu builds for its six largest accounts and for principals who are not its customers.

Three: build the cheap retailer side

Fund WhatsApp order capture at ₹34 lakh, returns at ₹60 lakh and languages at reduced scope, betting that retailer order volume is the real engine of usage revenue and the real defence against the platforms. Exhibit 6 suggests a per-order fee could be worth more than any licence uplift on the menu. But this builds what the paying customers explicitly refused to fund, on a biased sample and a thirty-one-person survey run by sales.

Four: re-run the exercise properly

Re-price the menu at September estimates, set the pool at 700 coins to match real capacity, invite a wider and differently chosen set of customers, and run it again in early November — slipping the lock three weeks into the Diwali freeze and arriving at the board with a process instead of a plan.

What none of the four does is question the list itself. Vikram's ledger refactor is on nobody's menu. The Saudi expansion is on nobody's menu. Embedded credit could not be estimated, so it sat on the menu at a price that may be meaningless, and three customers bought it anyway.

Deadline and constraints

The roadmap locks at nine on Monday, 12 October, because the Diwali code freeze runs from 4 to 15 November and anything not started by the third week of October will not ship before March. Discretionary capacity is ₹140 lakh and Farida will not move it; the two Pune resignations, which Meghna does not yet know about, will cut it further. The Shireen Foods commitment is contractual, with a ₹35 lakh credit and a 31 December deadline. The GST work is statutory. Tijori's tranche is conditional on net revenue retention reaching 118 per cent, currently 109. Embedded credit cannot be built as designed until an NBFC partner is signed and legal returns its review. The DPDP Act requires retailer consent for any store-level data passed to principals — precisely what stock visibility does. And twenty-four distributors who spent an afternoon in Ahmedabad are expecting to be told what their coins bought.

Questions for discussion

  1. What did the buy-a-feature exercise actually measure on 7 August, and what did the participants believe they were deciding?
  2. Exhibit 2 and Exhibit 4 are the same spending, counted twice. Which is the more legitimate reading, and what does your answer imply about who a software company's customer is?
  3. Exhibit 5 says the price at which nineteen customers bought the winning item was wrong by ₹160 lakh. Does a purchase made at a wrong price carry any information? If so, what?
  4. Meghna distributed 2,400 coins against a discretionary capacity worth 700. How should the currency and the menu have been designed, and what would have changed?
  5. Retailers spent heavily on items distributors refused to fund (Exhibit 3), and Exhibit 6 hints that retailer volume may carry the better revenue model. How should a two-sided product weigh the preferences of a party that pays nothing — and how much should Lena's own caveat about her sample change that weighing?
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Meghna put on the locked roadmap, what does she say to the twenty-four customers who spent coins in August, and what does she tell the board on Friday about how this company decides what to build?

Sunday, eleven o'clock

Meghna printed the four options and put them face down. On the way out she stopped at the whiteboard where somebody had written the August result in marker — the nineteen, the eighty-coin margin, the tick against multi-principal settlement — with a small smiley beside it, drawn when it had all seemed to have worked. She thought about the message from Nagpur, ₹41 lakh stuck since March, and about the retailers in Exhibit 3 who had spent a quarter of their coins asking to place orders on WhatsApp, which is where they were placing them anyway. She thought about Vikram's two engineers, working since July on something nobody had approved and everything on the menu depended on.

The guard locked the gate behind her at twenty past eleven. In nine hours she would have to say a number out loud.

Vetan Cloud and the Workshop Rupees

Pune, June 2026

On a warm Friday evening in June 2026, Ananya Kulkarni sat at her desk on the fourth floor of Vetan Cloud's Pune office, the window open to traffic easing on Baner Road, and read the same spreadsheet for the fourth time. In eleven days she would present the product roadmap for the next two quarters at Vetan Connect, the company's annual customer conference at the Bengaluru International Exhibition Centre, to four hundred HR heads, finance controllers and a handful of investors. Before that, on Monday morning, she had to walk into the leadership sync with a locked list of what the engineering team would build between July and September. The exercise she had run three weeks earlier to settle exactly this question had produced an answer that cost more than the budget she had been given to spend it.

Vetan Cloud

Vetan Cloud began in 2016 when three engineers — two from Pune's manufacturing sector and one who had built payroll systems inside a Bengaluru business process outsourcing firm — grew frustrated with how many small and mid-sized Indian employers still ran payroll on spreadsheets and outside consultants, chasing Provident Fund and ESI deadlines by hand every month. The company built a cloud payroll and statutory-compliance platform that computed salaries and tax deducted at source, filed Provident Fund and ESI returns with the EPFO and state labour departments, and kept pace as the Union government folded older labour laws into the four new Labour Codes. By 2026, Vetan Cloud served 3,800 employers across India, from twenty-employee retailers to thousand-employee manufacturing groups, and had followed several Indian-origin business houses into the Gulf, where they ran payroll for UAE and Saudi entities alongside their Indian ones. Annual recurring revenue stood at ₹42 crore, growing 34 percent a year, in a market that also held greytHR, Keka HR, Zoho People's payroll module, and RazorpayX Payroll, which bundled payroll with a banking relationship customers already had. Ananya, employee eleven and now head of product, believed Vetan Cloud's edge was never features but trust, and every roadmap had to protect that trust while still growing the product.

The situation

Every roadmap cycle at Vetan Cloud had historically been settled by whoever argued loudest in the leadership meeting, and Ananya had grown tired of watching the same three or four vocal accounts decide what engineering spent a quarter building. For the April cycle she tried something borrowed from a workshop she had once attended at ISB: buy-a-feature. She invited the eighteen largest employers on the platform — a cohort accounting for ₹19.2 crore of Vetan Cloud's ARR, well under half its customer count but close to half its revenue — to a half-day session on the sidelines of a compliance seminar in Bengaluru. Each customer's HR or finance representative received a card worth 100 workshop rupees, play money to be spent, alone or pooled with others at the table, across eight candidate features for the July release, shown in Exhibit 1. The prices were not arbitrary: Priya Deshpande, who led the Bengaluru engineering pod, and her counterpart in Pune had converted each feature's estimated build cost into workshop rupees at a fixed rate, so a price reflected roughly how many engineer-weeks the feature would consume. No single customer's 100 rupees could buy any feature outright; every item needed at least two customers, usually several, to pool their cards and agree it mattered enough to fund together — the entire point of the exercise. It would surface not what one insistent account wanted, but what a critical mass of paying customers, forced to choose, actually valued.

Devika Rao, Vetan Cloud's data scientist in Toronto, tallied the results and flagged something Ananya kept returning to. Eighteen customers spending 1,800 workshop rupees against a menu priced at 2,040 could never fund everything: three items cleared their price comfortably, shown in Exhibit 2, while the rest fell well short. But one winner, Devika noted, had been funded almost entirely by five accounts belonging to a single business group.

The people around the table

Devika Rao — data scientist, Toronto
She built the model turning workshop-rupee spending into a ranked list, and was first to notice that the top vote-getter, multi-entity consolidated payroll, had been funded almost entirely by five subsidiaries of one customer, Falak Apparel Group, an Indian-origin garment conglomerate with factories in Tiruppur and a trading arm in Dubai. Her worry was not that Falak had gamed the exercise — nothing stopped affiliated entities from pooling cards — but that a workshop meant to reveal broad preference could still be swung by one large account with several representatives present, and she wanted Ananya to weigh that before treating the ranking as settled.
Rajiv Menon — head of sales, New Jersey
Rajiv covered Vetan Cloud's small United States and Gulf pipeline and saw the same fact differently. Falak Apparel Group was mid-renewal, worth ₹2.6 crore in annual revenue if Vetan Cloud could consolidate payroll across its nine legal entities in India and the UAE onto one console; the group's finance chief had told him directly that without that feature, Falak would move the work to a rival that already offered it. To Rajiv, the workshop had simply confirmed in numbers what he already knew from the field, and he wanted the feature committed publicly at Vetan Connect.
Marcus Lindgren — customer-success lead, Singapore
Marcus worried about a quieter constituency: mid-market manufacturing and retail customers across Coimbatore, Nashik and Indore who had no seat at the Bengaluru table but who, through their larger peers, had still pushed the multi-state minimum-wage auto-updater to a comfortable win. His renewal calls through May carried the same complaint — every state minimum-wage revision meant updating pay structures by hand before the payroll run — and two accounts had named it as a reason they were evaluating greytHR. He did not want that signal diluted by an argument about who had funded what.
Priya Deshpande — engineering lead, Bengaluru
Priya held the number that made the disagreement concrete. Q3's engineering capacity for new feature work, after support and platform maintenance across the Bengaluru and Pune pods, came to ₹90 lakh, and she would not commit her team to more, whatever the workshop or the sales pipeline wanted.

Three ways forward

Option One: Fund the ranking exactly as spent

Commit all three items that cleared their price — consolidated payroll, the minimum-wage updater and gig billing — ₹110 lakh against a ₹90 lakh budget, closing the gap by deferring a July compliance patch or hiring contract engineers in Pune. The upside is a roadmap that is exactly what paying customers asked for. The cost is treating a play-money exercise as more binding than the engineering ceiling, and delaying a patch tied to a fixed government deadline.

Option Two: Protect the largest account

Fund consolidated payroll in full to secure the ₹2.6 crore Falak Apparel Group renewal, and spend the remaining ₹52 lakh on gig billing, setting the minimum-wage updater aside until Q4. This gives Rajiv a concrete commitment to close a difficult renewal. Its cost is that it overrides the exercise's own purpose: fourteen of eighteen customers, most nowhere near Falak's size, funded the minimum-wage item, and Marcus already has two accounts naming that gap as a reason to evaluate a rival. Choosing revenue concentration over revealed breadth risks exactly the churn Marcus is watching for.

Option Three: Let the margins break the tie

Fund the two items that cleared their price with the widest margins and broadest bases — consolidated payroll and the minimum-wage updater, ₹80 lakh combined, leaving ₹10 lakh of headroom under Priya's ceiling. Defer gig billing, whose ten-rupee margin and four-customer base were the weakest of the three winners, to the October workshop for a fair re-test with more staffing-sector customers present. This keeps both Rajiv's and Marcus's commitments intact, respects Priya's budget without a side deal, and gives the deferred item a second hearing instead of a unilateral cut.

Questions for discussion

  1. What did buy-a-feature let Vetan Cloud learn that an open feature-request list or a RICE-scored backlog could not, and why did it need paying customers, not employees, to reveal it?
  2. Exhibit 3 shows consolidated payroll was funded mostly by five entities from one group. Does that concentration weaken the result, and what should Ananya change about the next workshop?
  3. Compare Option Two and Option Three. Both protect Falak Apparel Group. What differs in how each treats the minimum-wage signal, and why does it matter for Marcus's mid-market customers?
  4. If you were Ananya, what would you say on Monday to justify deferring gig labour billing, given that it was, on the workshop's own terms, a funded item?

A note for the learner

Buy-a-feature exists because what employers say they want is not what they will pay for out of a fixed budget. Given an open request list, most customers ask for everything, and most scoring frameworks — RICE included — turn that wish list into a number without ever forcing a trade-off, so the ranking reflects whoever wrote the most persuasive justification, not real preference. Buy-a-feature fixes this with a budget that is genuinely scarce, priced to reflect real build cost, and asks customers to choose among each other, in the open. Its value over a survey or an advisory vote is that customers must reveal what they will give up, not just what they would like, and pooling forces conversations a product team could never arrange on its own.

A well-reasoned answer treats the workshop's output as evidence, not verdict. It reads Exhibit 2 the way Ananya must — not only which items crossed their price, but by how much, since a margin of ten workshop rupees funded by four customers in one sector is a weaker signal than a margin of forty funded broadly, even though a simple ranking counts both as wins. It also takes Devika's caution about Falak Apparel Group's five entities seriously without discarding the result: a large customer pooling its affiliates' budgets is not fraud, it is exactly the trade-off pooling allows. The real question is whether the mid-market voice, with no comparable way to concentrate its budget, was still heard — and Exhibit 3 suggests it was, since the minimum-wage updater drew fourteen of eighteen customers on its own.

The defensible path is Option Three. It resolves the ₹90 lakh ceiling using the workshop's own information rather than opinion or account pressure: the two items with the widest margins and broadest bases are funded now, the one that barely cleared its price on a narrow base is deferred and re-tested rather than killed, and both Rajiv's renewal and Marcus's churn risk are addressed without either overriding the exercise. The lesson is not that buy-a-feature removes the need for judgment — Priya's budget still forces a cut — but that the same exercise revealing what customers value also shows, in its margins and coalitions, how much to trust each result, a sounder basis for that cut than blind adherence to the raw list or a single stakeholder's override.

Buy-a-Feature

What customers choose when they have to spend a limited budget — and why that is a different question from what they say they want.

1. A room in Bengaluru, and a list nobody agrees on

On the morning of 18 September 2025, Devika Rao, Vice-President of Product at Uttung Warehouse Cloud, sat in a glass meeting room in Baner, Pune, with a printed backlog of nineteen candidate features and engineering capacity for roughly four of them. Uttung sells warehouse management software to mid-market Indian distributors — pharmaceutical wholesalers, apparel exporters, food and beverage companies with three to fifteen warehouses each. The company had ended the previous financial year at about ₹42 crore of annual recurring revenue across 340 customers, growing at a rate that made the next two quarters of the roadmap consequential rather than academic.

The nineteen items had arrived from four directions and the four directions did not agree. Sales wanted automated reconciliation of GST e-invoices and e-way bills, which two large prospects had raised in deals. Support wanted a rebuilt dashboard, on the grounds that it generated the most tickets. Engineering wanted an open API, because every integration request was currently a bespoke project. And the loudest single voice belonged to the chief executive of Trikaal Pharma Distribution, an Ahmedabad customer paying ₹38 lakh a year, who had written to Uttung's CEO on 4 September asking why the reconciliation work had slipped twice.

Devika had run the usual instruments and distrusted all of them. A survey of 96 customers had returned an average importance score above 4.1 out of 5 for eleven of the nineteen items; when everything is important, nothing is. A weighted scoring sheet had produced a ranking that changed whenever she changed a weight, and she could not defend any particular set of weights to her own CEO, let alone to Trikaal's. What she had was a set of opinions about value, each held sincerely, none of them tested against a constraint.

So she booked a room in Bengaluru for 9 October, invited operations heads from eight customers, and prepared to hand each of them a hundred lakh rupees of play money and a price list. The stakes were ordinary and therefore real: roughly ₹3.2 crore of engineering payroll over two quarters, one escalated relationship, and the credibility of a product function that had already told the field twice that it was "working on prioritisation".

2. The idea, stated precisely

Buy-a-feature is a structured group exercise in which customers are given a fixed, deliberately insufficient budget of play money and a priced list of candidate features, and must spend that budget to get the things they want. Each feature carries a price. The prices are set so that the total price list costs substantially more than the sum of all the budgets in the room, and so that the most expensive items cost more than any single participant can afford. Participants may pool their money. The output is not only the totals but the argument — the recorded conversation in which one customer persuades another to co-fund something.

The problem it was invented to solve is stated-preference inflation. When you ask a person to rate the importance of a feature, the question has no cost attached, so the rational answer is to say yes to everything that might conceivably help; the respondent bears none of the consequence of their own enthusiasm. The device that fixes this is the budget constraint, which converts a rating into a trade-off. In economics the underlying principle is revealed preference — the idea, formalised by Paul Samuelson in 1938, that what a chooser gives up to obtain something tells you more about their valuation than what they say about it. Conjoint analysis, developed by Paul Green and Vithala Rao in 1971, applies the same logic statistically by forcing respondents to choose between bundles rather than rate attributes.

Buy-a-feature is the cheap, qualitative, human version of that logic. It was popularised by Luke Hohmann in Innovation Games (2006) as one of a family of collaborative-play techniques for eliciting customer requirements, and it spread through agile product circles in the decade that followed because it needs no statistician, runs in an afternoon, and produces something that a room full of executives will actually believe: a photograph of customers putting money on the table.

The sentence Devika could say in a meeting without sounding glib: “We are not asking customers to rate features. We are making them pay for them, because a ranking with no budget is a wish list, and a purchase is a trade-off.”

Note carefully what the definition does not claim. It does not claim to measure willingness to pay in real money. It does not claim the room is representative of the market. It claims one thing only: that within this room, with these prices, these people gave up these alternatives to get these things. Everything useful about the technique and every way it goes wrong follows from taking that sentence literally.

3. How it actually works, step by step

The mechanics look trivial and are not, because three of the steps are design decisions disguised as logistics. Devika's preparation ran as follows.

Choose and phrase the list. She cut nineteen candidates to ten, discarding items that were mandatory regardless of customer opinion and items too vague to price. Each surviving item was written as an outcome in the customer's language — "enforce first-expiry-first-out picking so short-dated stock cannot ship last" rather than "FEFO module". A price list of solutions invites customers to buy a technology they do not understand; a price list of outcomes invites them to buy a result they can feel.

Price the list by cost, not by importance. This is the step that most teams get wrong and the one that determines what the exercise can teach. Uttung's prices were derived from engineering's build estimates, scaled so that one lakh of play money represented roughly one engineer-week. Because the price is effort and the spending is value, the ratio of money attracted to price is a customer-generated value-per-unit-of-effort number. That is the direct link to the value-versus-effort matrix, the technique buy-a-feature extends: in a value-effort matrix, the product manager estimates both axes; in buy-a-feature, the customers supply the value axis and engineering supplies the effort axis, and neither gets to grade its own homework.

Set the budget so that it visibly bites. Uttung's ten features totalled ₹2,240 lakh of play money. Eight participants with ₹100 lakh each put ₹800 lakh in the room — about 36 per cent of the list. Practitioners generally aim for 30 to 50 per cent. Above that the constraint stops biting and customers simply fund most things; below about 25 per cent the exercise becomes a lottery in which nothing can be afforded and participants disengage.

Choose the room. Eight operations heads, all from distributors of comparable size, none accompanied by their account executive from Uttung. The sampling decision is the largest single source of error in the whole method and it is made silently, on an invitation list, weeks before anyone spends anything.

Run it, and record the argument. Forty-five minutes of spending, out loud, with coalitions permitted and encouraged: the expensive items can only be bought by two or three customers combining. A facilitator notes who moved money, when, and what they said to persuade someone else. Afterwards, a debrief in which each participant explains their largest single bet.

4. The worked example, line by line

On 9 October the eight customers spent as shown below. Each row is a feature with its price in play lakh; each column is one customer's allocation. Every column sums to exactly 100, because the facilitator required participants to spend their whole budget — leaving money unspent is a way of avoiding the trade-off.

Read the totals column first and one fact jumps out: nothing was fully funded. The largest single total, ₹135 lakh against F4's price of ₹260 lakh, is barely half. A naive reading rule — build whatever the customers bought outright — would therefore produce an empty roadmap. This is normal and it is why the arithmetic matters. With a budget set at 36 per cent of the list, the expected funding level of an average item is also about 36 per cent; full funding only happens where demand is heavily concentrated.

The useful quantity is the funding ratio: money attracted divided by price. Because the price is engineering effort, the ratio is customer-revealed value per unit of effort. That single observation was worth the cost of the workshop. The item that had consumed the most executive attention in September was the item its own champion would not pay for when the money had to come from somewhere. Devika did not conclude that Trikaal's CEO was lying; she concluded, correctly, that the CEO had been describing a commercial irritation and the operations head had been describing an operational one, and that the two were not the same thing.

Second pass: change one input and watch the ranking move

Ten days later, engineering revisited F2. Rather than building a reconciliation engine, they could route filings through the GST Suvidha Provider integration Uttung already maintained and reconcile against the returned invoice reference numbers. The estimate fell from 420 to 180 — from roughly 84 engineer-weeks to 36.

The lazy second pass is to divide the old money by the new price: 45 ÷ 180 = 0.25, which lifts F2 from tenth to eighth and changes nothing. The honest second pass is to re-run the purchase, because demand was measured at a price. Devika re-ran the three cold-chain customers over a video call on 22 October with F2 repriced. Trikaal moved to 40 on F2 and cut FEFO from 60 to 45; Tarangini Foods went to 35 on F2, cutting cold-chain alerts from 40 to 30; Tapan Cold Chain put in 15. F2 now attracted 90 against a price of 180 — a ratio of 0.50, and a doubling of absolute demand from a halving of price.

Three lessons sit inside that small table. First, the technique measures value at a price, not value in the abstract; the same feature can be unwanted at 420 and contested at 180. Second, the ranking is therefore only as good as engineering's estimates, which means a buy-a-feature output is a joint product of customer preference and internal cost belief, and a re-estimate is grounds for re-running the exercise rather than re-doing the division. Third, money is conserved: F2's gain of 45 came out of F7 and F4, so the apparent "strength" of the cold-chain cluster in round one was partly an artefact of having nothing better to spend on.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Play money is not willingness to pay. The budget constraint removes the "everything is a five" problem, but it does not tell you what anyone would pay in rupees. A customer who allocates 40 per cent of a play budget to expiry-date enforcement has told you that expiry outranks pick-path optimisation for them; they have not told you that they would pay ₹4 lakh a year for it, and if you need that number you must ask a different question — a price test, a paid pilot, or a contractual commitment. Conflating relative preference with absolute value is the most common overreach, and it is usually committed by the person presenting the results rather than the person who ran them.

Your prices are your effort estimates, in disguise. Because the price list encodes engineering cost, every systematic estimation bias becomes a systematic bias in the customer's answer. Teams that habitually under-estimate platform work will under-price it, which makes platform work look cheap, which makes it attract money it would not attract at its true cost. The discipline is to have prices derived by engineers who have not seen the customer research, and to publish the estimate confidence alongside the price.

The room is the result. Sampling dominates everything else. Eight distributors in Bengaluru on a Thursday are not the market; they are the subset willing to travel, which skews towards engaged, mid-sized, well-run customers who like you. Churned customers and lost prospects — the two populations whose preferences would most change your roadmap — are structurally absent. The correct posture is to treat the output as evidence about a named segment, and to say the segment's name out loud every time you quote the result.

The transcript is worth more than the totals. The numbers say F8 attracted four backers; the recording says why. Tundi Steel wanted the open API because their Tally-based accounting reconciliation was manual; Tasveer Home Retail wanted it to push stock positions to their own marketplace listings on ONDC. Those are different features wearing one name, and a team that reads only the totals will build one of them and disappoint two customers. The habit that separates practitioners is writing down the sentence each buyer used when they moved money.

Cheap items win on ratio, and that is only sometimes right. F9, the handheld app in Hindi, Marathi and Tamil, topped the ratio table on ₹70 lakh from two buyers. A ratio ranking systematically favours small items, because small denominators are volatile and because a cheap item is an easy place to park leftover money. The corrective is to read ratio and breadth together: F9's 0.78 rests on two backers, while F8's 0.55 rests on four. A defensible rule is to require both a ratio above the room average and a minimum number of independent backers.

It cannot see what is not on the list. Buy-a-feature is a closed-choice instrument. If no card says "the system is slow at month-end", slowness receives no money and will appear, falsely, to be a non-issue. Worse, the technique is structurally blind to what the Kano model calls delighters — capabilities customers cannot imagine wanting because they have never seen them. Customers reliably fund improvements to the job they are doing today; they almost never fund the reframing of that job. Every serious practitioner pairs buy-a-feature with an open-ended discovery method and treats the two as answering different questions.

Attendance is a political fact. In business-to-business products the person who accepts a workshop invitation is rarely the economic buyer and is often the person with the least urgent calendar. An operations head funds what makes their week easier; a chief financial officer funds what shows up in working capital. If you seat one role type, you have measured one role type's preferences. And if an account executive sits at the table, the customer's spending becomes a performance for their vendor relationship rather than an expression of need.

It ranks; it does not schedule. A funded item may be blocked by a dependency, may collide with a compliance deadline, or may belong to a quarter already committed. More importantly, mandatory work should never appear on the price list at all. Devika deliberately kept obligations under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act off the list: asking customers whether to fund a legal requirement teaches you nothing and, if they decline to fund it, creates a document you will regret.

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and the effect of company stage

In business-to-business software the technique is at home. Customers already think in budgets, already have committees, and already expect to be consulted; assembling eight of them is a day's work and the same eight will have opinions about the results for a year. The characteristic failure is not methodological but political: the workshop becomes a customer-council ritual in which the vendor confirms what it already intended to build, and participants gradually learn that their spending changes nothing.

In consumer products the economics invert. Eight users cannot represent ten million, recruitment cost per unit of signal is high, and the same question can often be answered more cheaply and more reliably by an experiment. Buy-a-feature earns its place in consumer work where experimentation is impossible — before anything is built, when the choice is between four expensive directions, or in regulated categories where you cannot A/B test with real money. There, the exercise runs online with points rather than notes, on a recruited panel, and is read as structured qualitative evidence rather than as a measurement.

Marketplaces present a subtler problem: the two sides want opposite things. On a home-services marketplace, professionals will fund control over pricing and lead quality while consumers will fund transparency and faster response — and some features one side funds are features the other would pay to prevent. The only defensible design is separate tables per side, separate price lists where the build cost differs, and an explicit refusal to add the two sides' totals into a single ranking. A merged ranking silently assigns a weight to each side's welfare while pretending to be arithmetic.

Stage changes the meaning of the output more than it changes the mechanics. At an early-stage company with thirty customers, eight of them in a room represent a quarter of the business, so the exercise doubles as revenue-retention work and the results are nearly binding — with the attendant danger of building exquisitely for the customers you happen to have rather than the segment you intend to serve. At a company of Uttung's size, and more so at a large one, a single room cannot carry the roadmap; the output is one segment's evidence, to be weighed against platform obligations, compliance deadlines and strategy. There, buy-a-feature's real function is narrower and still valuable: it breaks deadlocks between functions who are each arguing from anecdote, by producing a fact that neither of them controls.

7. Common mistakes, and the cheapest diagnostic for each

Pricing by importance instead of by cost. The symptom, visible from outside, is a price list in which the items everyone knows are strategic happen to be the expensive ones. The underlying misunderstanding is treating price as a proxy for value, which makes the exercise circular: customers then re-rank a ranking you already made. The cheapest diagnostic is to ask two engineers who have not seen the customer research to re-derive the prices from build estimates, and to compare the two lists item by item. Any item whose price moves by more than a factor of two was priced by opinion.

A budget that does not bite. The symptom is a cheerful, conflict-free workshop in which most items get funded and everybody leaves happy. The misunderstanding is that the goal is customer satisfaction rather than information; information comes only from the refusals. The diagnostic is arithmetic and takes ten seconds: divide total budget by total price list before the session. If the figure is above roughly 50 per cent, raise the prices or cut the budget.

Mixing incompatible segments at one table. The symptom is a spending pattern with almost no overlap — every participant funding a different item alone, few coalitions, and a debrief in which people talk past each other. The misunderstanding is that more variety in the room means a more representative result; in fact heterogeneity destroys the coalition mechanism that makes the technique informative. The diagnostic is to look at the allocation matrix and count items with three or more backers. In Uttung's session four items cleared that bar, which is healthy; had the number been zero or one, the room held two markets rather than one.

Treating the output as a commitment. The symptom appears three weeks later, in an email asking when the feature the customer "bought" will ship. The misunderstanding is the customer's, but it was created by the vendor's silence. The diagnostic is to reread the invitation: if it did not state in writing that the exercise informs prioritisation and does not constitute a delivery commitment, the expectation was set by default. The cost of catching this late is measured in trust, which is the one input to this technique you cannot re-buy.

8. What good looks like

A well-run version of this decision looks unglamorous. The backlog is cut to between ten and fifteen outcomes written in customer language. Prices come from blind engineering estimates and are published with their uncertainty. The budget is set at a third of the list and the shortfall is announced at the start, so participants understand that refusing things is the point. The room is segment-homogeneous, and where there are two segments there are two rooms. No vendor salesperson sits at the table. The session is recorded, and the coalition conversations are transcribed and quoted in the write-up alongside the totals.

Afterwards the numbers are read with two columns, not one: funding ratio for efficiency, backer count for breadth. The result is placed next to a conventional value-versus-effort view and the two are compared explicitly, with disagreements between them investigated rather than averaged away. Mandatory and platform work is kept off the list and funded separately, out of a protected capacity allocation. Within ten working days the participants receive a written note saying what was funded, what was not, and what the company has decided not to build at all — because the decision not to build, communicated honestly, is what earns the right to invite the same people back next year.

9. What Devika decided

On 30 October, Devika committed the next two quarters to four items: first-expiry-first-out enforcement, bin-level cycle counting, the open API and webhooks, and the multilingual handheld app, which she added as a low-cost companion to the cycle-counting release rather than as a standalone bet. Her stated rule was a funding ratio above the room average of 0.36 combined with at least three independent backers — a rule that admitted F7, F1 and F8, and excluded F9 on breadth. She overrode her own rule for F9 and said so in writing, on the grounds that it cost nine engineer-weeks, that both backers employed warehouse staff who did not read English comfortably, and that the risk of being wrong was small and reversible.

She did the GST reconciliation work as well — but off the price list, funded from the compliance allocation, and re-scoped to the ₹180 lakh design. When she met Trikaal Pharma's chief executive on 6 November she took Exhibit 1 with her and showed him that his own operations head had put fifteen of a hundred behind reconciliation and sixty behind expiry enforcement. The conversation that followed was about short-dated stock, which was the real problem, and the escalation did not recur.

What to learn next, and why. Value versus effort is the parent idea: buy-a-feature is a value-versus-effort matrix in which the customers fill in the value axis, so understanding how the effort axis is estimated tells you exactly how much the whole exercise can be trusted. The Kano model is the necessary complement, because it names the category — delighters — that buy-a-feature is structurally incapable of detecting. And saying no is the skill the technique creates demand for: a workshop that produces a ranking without producing a published list of refusals has generated expectations without generating decisions.

Two questions to sit with.

  1. If the eight customers in Devika's room had been the eight who churned in the previous year rather than eight who renewed, which items on Exhibit 1 would you expect to move most — and what does your answer imply about how you should describe this result to your board?
  2. Engineering's re-estimate changed F2's price from 420 to 180 and changed the answer. Under what conditions is a result that moves when your cost estimate moves a sign that the method is working, and under what conditions is it a sign that the method is measuring your own uncertainty back at you?
Uttung Warehouse Cloud, Trikaal Pharma Distribution, Tapan Cold Chain, Tarangini Foods, Ulhas Beverages, Uttaran Apparel, Tasveer Home Retail, Tehzeeb Furnishings and Tundi Steel Traders are fictional companies created for teaching purposes. Named regulations, statutes and public infrastructure are real and are used as market context only. All figures are illustrative.

Buy-a-Feature

Letting customers spend a fixed budget to reveal real preferences — the mechanics, the second-order effects, the situations in which the method actively misleads, and the arguments the field has not settled.

1. Two decisions, eight weeks apart

On 4 February 2026, Rukmini Iyer, Head of Product at Tatvik Health Systems in Chennai, had a roadmap review in nine days and a disagreement she could not adjudicate. Tatvik sells operating-theatre scheduling and surgical-inventory software to hospital groups — sixty customers, about ₹96 crore of annual recurring revenue, contracts between ₹40 lakh and ₹4.2 crore a year. Seven candidate items competed for two quarters of a forty-person engineering organisation. Sales wanted interoperability with hospital information systems under the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission standards, because three live deals had raised it. The customer-success team wanted automated evidence packs for NABH accreditation audits, because four smaller hospitals had asked. Rukmini's largest customer, Trilok Hospitals Group in Coimbatore, wanted the theatre auto-optimiser, which cost more than the other six items put together at the margin.

Every instrument she owned returned an answer she could not defend. A weighted scoring sheet ranked interoperability first when strategic fit carried 30 per cent and ranked it fourth when it carried 15, and no one in the building could justify either weight. So she booked a half-day in Hyderabad on 20 February, invited operating heads from six hospital groups, and prepared to hand each of them play money and a price list.

Eight weeks later and 350 kilometres south-west, Kabir Sethi, Director of Product at Tarasvi Bazaar in Bengaluru, was preparing the same exercise with a structurally different problem. Tarasvi is a two-sided marketplace for home services — deep cleaning, appliance repair, pest control — operating in fourteen cities with about 180,000 monthly transacting consumers and 22,000 partner professionals. Take rate had drifted from 21 per cent to 18 per cent over four quarters as professionals learned to complete second and third jobs for the same household off-platform. Kabir's backlog held five contested items. Three of them appeared, word for word, on both the consumer wish list and the professional wish list — and he suspected, without evidence he could show anyone, that the two sides wanted opposite things from the same words.

Rukmini's problem was that she had too few customers and each had a different amount of money. Kabir's problem was that he had two customer populations whose interests were partly opposed and a third interest — the platform's own — that neither population would ever fund. Both reached for the same technique. It is worth being precise about what that technique can and cannot do for either of them.

2. The idea, its history, and the four camps

Buy-a-feature is a structured group elicitation in which participants receive a fixed, deliberately insufficient budget of play money and a priced list of candidate capabilities, and must spend the budget to obtain what they want; prices are set so that the total list costs far more than the money in the room and the largest items exceed any individual budget, forcing both refusal and coalition. The observable outputs are three: the allocation matrix, the coalition transcript, and the refusals.

The problem it was built to solve is stated-preference inflation. An unconstrained importance rating has no opportunity cost, so the dominant strategy for a respondent is enthusiasm about everything; the resulting instrument has almost no discriminating power. The economic corrective is revealed preference — Paul Samuelson's 1938 formulation that what a chooser surrenders to obtain something is better evidence of valuation than what they assert about it. Choice-based conjoint analysis, introduced by Paul Green and Vithala Rao in 1971, industrialised the same insight statistically: force respondents to choose between whole bundles, then infer part-worth utilities. Mechanism design supplied a parallel tradition — William Vickrey's 1961 auction work and the Clarke–Groves family of mechanisms that make honest revelation of value the participant's best strategy — and prediction markets, from the Iowa Electronic Markets in 1988 onward, supplied the intuition that a market price aggregates dispersed private information better than a poll.

Buy-a-feature is the informal, low-cost, human-scale descendant of these. Its immediate ancestor in software practice is cumulative voting — the "hundred-dollar test" described by Dean Leffingwell and Don Widrig in Managing Software Requirements (1999) — in which stakeholders distribute a hundred points across requirements. Luke Hohmann's Innovation Games (2006) added the two elements that make the technique interesting: prices, which anchor the exercise to cost and make the output a value-per-effort ratio rather than a popularity score, and coalitions, which turn a private allocation into a public negotiation that can be recorded.

That lineage explains why competent practitioners disagree so sharply about what the output means. Four positions are held by serious people, and each would sign a different proposition.

3. Mechanics in depth, including the parts usually left implicit

The visible mechanics — cards, money, a facilitator — take an afternoon to learn. The design decisions underneath them determine the answer, and three of them are usually made without anyone noticing that a decision was made.

Pricing. Prices should be proportional to build cost, not to importance. Tatvik used one lakh of play money per engineer-week. Because the denominator is effort and the numerator is customer money, the funding ratio is customer-supplied value per unit of effort — which is precisely the value-versus-effort matrix with the value axis outsourced to the people who experience the value. When prices are instead set by the product manager's sense of importance, the exercise becomes circular: participants re-rank a ranking the vendor already made, and the output confirms the input.

Endowment. Who gets how much money is a concealed welfare judgement. Equal budgets implement one-customer-one-vote. Budgets proportional to contract value implement one-rupee-one-vote. These produce different rankings whenever large and small customers want different things — which, in enterprise software, is almost always. Very few teams can state which rule they used or why, and the choice is usually made by whoever printed the envelopes.

Scarcity. Define B as total money in the room and P as the total price of the list. The design parameter is B / P. Above roughly 0.5 the constraint stops biting, most items get funded, and the session degenerates into a pleasant confirmation of the backlog. Below about 0.2 nothing is affordable, participants disengage, and spending becomes arbitrary. Practitioners target 0.3 to 0.4.

The arithmetic worth knowing

For each item i, let mₑ be money attracted and pₑ its price.

Funding ratio  rₑ = mₑ / pₑ — customer-revealed value per unit of effort.

Lift  Lₑ = rₑ ÷ (B / P) — how much more money the item attracted than money spread evenly across the list in proportion to price would predict. L = 1 is exactly what random spending produces; only items well above 1 carry information.

Effective backers  Nₑ = 1 / Σ s², where s is each backer's share of that item's money — the inverse Herfindahl index. An item funded ₹100 by one buyer and ₹100 by another has N = 2; one funded ₹190 and ₹10 has N = 1.1 and is, in substance, one customer's request wearing a coalition's clothes.

Three second-order effects distinguish practitioners who have run the exercise more than twice. The first is price elasticity of play demand: an item's money is a function of its price, so a re-estimate does not license re-dividing the old money by the new price — it licenses re-running the purchase. Halving a price routinely doubles or triples the money attracted, because the item moves from unaffordable to coalition-fundable. The second is menu dependence. Money is conserved, so every item's score depends on which other items are on the list; adding an eighth card changes all seven existing scores, and scores from two workshops with different lists cannot be compared. This is a violation of the independence of irrelevant alternatives, and it is the reason funding ratios should never be tracked as a time series. The third is sequence contamination: whichever card the facilitator discusses first attracts disproportionate money, an ordinary anchoring effect, which is why careful teams randomise card order across tables and check whether position predicts spend.

4. When the method applies, and when it misleads

The conditions are best stated as claims that can be checked before the session rather than as advice. Six of them matter, and they discriminate sharply between Rukmini's situation and Kabir's.

Claim one: the candidate items are substitutes competing for one budget in the participant's own mind. For Tatvik this holds — a hospital chief operating officer genuinely trades theatre utilisation against accreditation readiness, because both consume the same management attention. For Tarasvi it holds on the consumer side and fails on the supply side, where same-day payout is a cash-flow matter and job-locality choice is a time matter, and a professional does not experience them as competing.

Claim two: the participants personally experience the value. True for Tatvik's operating heads and for both of Kabir's populations. It is false for a procurement officer, a channel partner, or a systems integrator, whose incentives run through the purchase rather than the use.

Claim three: build cost is knowable in advance to within roughly a factor of two. This is the fragile one. Tatvik's items are conventional software; Rukmini's estimates were probably good to ±40 per cent. Tarasvi's fixed-price guarantee has a cost dominated not by engineering but by the expected value of the guarantee payouts, which nobody had modelled — so its price on the card was, in effect, a guess about a financial exposure dressed as an engineering estimate.

Claim four: item values are approximately independent of each other. Where items are complements the method breaks. An interoperability platform is worth little on its own and a great deal once three integrations exist on top of it; a participant who understands this cannot express it with a single allocation, and one who does not understand it will under-fund the platform every time. This is the single most reliable reason foundational work loses buy-a-feature sessions everywhere it is run.

Claim five: the room is the segment you intend to serve. Rukmini's six hospital groups are all existing, renewing customers; the two segments she is trying to win — large private chains running a competing scheduler, and government-scheme hospitals — were not in the room and could not be.

Claim six: the decision tolerates a sample of six to twelve. A reversible two-quarter bet does. A platform re-architecture, a pricing change, or a market-entry decision does not, and reaching for a workshop in those cases is a category error dressed as customer-centricity.

The method is actively misleading, rather than merely weak, in three situations. When values are distributional — one participant's gain is another's loss — the totals are a sum of incompatible quantities and the ranking is arithmetic performed on an ill-defined object. When the real question is what to stop rather than what to start, the exercise generates additional demand and no capacity. And when the item that matters most cannot be priced or is not on the list, its absence is read by everyone in the room, including the vendor, as evidence that it does not matter.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product portfolios. Asking a customer to allocate across product lines asks them to make a portfolio judgement they do not hold the profit-and-loss for. Participants reliably fund the product they personally use and starve the one their colleague uses. The workable design is one session per product with a shared price scale, and an explicit internal step afterwards in which the company — not the customer — allocates across products.

Two-sided markets. Kabir's case. Separate tables, separate price lists where build costs differ, and an absolute refusal to add the two sides' totals into one ranking. Adding them silently assigns a relative weight to each side's welfare while appearing to be arithmetic. Worse, there is a third party — the platform — whose interests neither side will fund. Nobody in a marketplace workshop ever funds anti-disintermediation work, trust-and-safety investment, or take-rate defence, because for participants those are costs, not features.

Regulated products. Compliance work should never appear on the price list. If Tatvik had priced a card for Digital Personal Data Protection Act obligations and the room had declined to fund it, Rukmini would own a document showing customers voted against a legal duty. Mandatory work is funded from a protected allocation off the board, and participants are told so at the start, which also prevents the common complaint that the vendor "ignored the vote".

Hardware plus software. Price ceases to be linear in engineer-weeks. A hardware revision carries tooling, bill-of-materials change, supplier qualification and, in India, BIS certification, with a lead time measured in quarters and a cost that can exceed the entire play budget in the room. Teams resolve this by quietly excluding hardware from the list — which guarantees that hardware problems receive no money and appear unimportant. Section 8 shows what that costs.

AI-native products. Three properties break the price list. Cost per item is dominated by inference spend and evaluation effort rather than build effort, and inference spend scales with usage rather than with the one-time build. Many "features" are not binary but thresholds on a continuum — extraction accuracy of 92 per cent versus 97 per cent is a different product at a very different price, and a card that says "better accuracy" is unpriceable. And model capability improves underneath you, so a price list written in January can be materially wrong by April. At Tathya AI Systems in Hyderabad, which sells document-extraction agents to lenders, the practical adaptation was to price cards as accuracy tiers with explicit numbers on them — "97 per cent field-level accuracy on hand-filled forms, audited monthly" — and to re-issue the price list every quarter, treating the list itself as a perishable good.

Organisational seams. The exercise crosses three functions and fails at the joins. Sales owns the customer relationship and therefore the invitation list, which means sales controls the sample. Engineering owns the estimates and therefore the prices, which means engineering controls the denominator. Product owns the interpretation and the communication of refusals, which is the only unpopular part. What mature companies actually do — as distinct from what they describe in conference talks — is pre-commit sixty to seventy per cent of capacity to platform, compliance and strategic work, and run the workshop only on the genuinely contested remainder. This is more honest than it sounds, and it makes the exercise better: a narrow list of comparable items is exactly the condition under which the method is informative.

6. Ten nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

1. Demand is measured at a price, not in the abstract. The tell-tale sign of the competent-but-not-expert practitioner is recomputing ratios after engineering re-estimates an item. The expert re-runs the purchase with the affected participants, because the old allocation was a response to the old price. The obvious reading — that value is a property of the feature — is wrong; value in this instrument is a property of the feature-price pair.

2. Scores are menu-dependent. An expert recognises this in the wild when someone proposes comparing this year's ratios with last year's, or merging results from two sessions with slightly different lists. Because budgets are conserved, an item's score is partly a statement about what else was available. The correct comparison is always within a single list.

3. The endowment rule is a concealed policy. The expert's first question on being shown results is not "what won" but "how much money did each participant get, and why?" Equal budgets favour the numerous small customer; revenue-weighted budgets favour the large one. Neither is correct in general, and an item that wins under both rules is a different and much stronger finding than one that wins under one.

4. Coalitions are the signal; totals are the summary. The expert asks who moved first, who was persuaded, and what argument did the persuading. A total of ₹150 lakh assembled by four independent buyers who did not talk to each other means something different from ₹150 lakh assembled after one participant spent ten minutes convincing three others. The first is aggregated private preference; the second is one articulate customer's opinion propagating through a room, and it is the commonest way a workshop launders a single voice into apparent consensus.

5. Cheap items are systematically over-ranked by ratio. Small denominators are volatile and cheap cards are a convenient home for leftover money that would otherwise go unspent. The tell is a ratio table whose top three entries are the three cheapest cards. The corrective is to read lift together with effective backers and to treat anything with fewer than three effective backers as one customer's request regardless of its ratio.

6. Role composition determines the answer more than company selection does. An operating head funds what makes this month easier; a finance director funds what shows up in working capital; a clinician funds what reduces the chance of harm. The expert asks for the job-title distribution before looking at any number, and treats a session of six operating heads as a measurement of operating-head preference, not of customer preference.

7. The interesting population is the one that did not attend. Churned customers, lost prospects and non-customers are exactly the groups whose preferences would most change a roadmap, and they are structurally absent from every customer workshop ever run. The expert's diagnostic question is "who declined the invitation, and what do they have in common?" — because the decline pattern is itself data.

8. Complements always lose. Foundational and platform items are under-funded in every session, not because customers are short-sighted but because the instrument requires each item to be valued standing alone. The expert recognises the pattern — an infrastructure card with a low ratio and one or two backers who happen to be the most technically sophisticated customers in the room — and knows that the correct response is to fund it off the board, not to argue with the result.

9. The method answers “which”, never “how much” or “when”. The tell is a slide translating funding ratios into revenue forecasts or into a quarterly plan. Play money has no exchange rate with rupees and the exercise contains no information about sequencing, dependencies or capacity. An expert who wants willingness-to-pay runs a price test or asks for a contractual commitment, and treats those as entirely separate studies.

10. The refusal list is the product. A workshop that generates a ranking but no published list of things the company has decided not to build has created expectations without creating decisions, and has spent customer goodwill to buy nothing. The expert's write-up leads with the refusals, names them, and sends them to participants within ten working days — which is uncomfortable, and is the reason the practice is rarer than the technique.

7. How it differs by product type and company stage — and where it does not

Begin with what does not change, because most published advice implies variation that is not there. The pricing rule, the scarcity ratio, the coalition mechanism and all ten nuances above are invariant across product types. What changes is only the economics of assembling a room and the meaning of the word "cost" in the denominator.

In business-to-business and enterprise software the method is at home: customers think in budgets, expect consultation, and will attend. Enterprise adds one distinctive hazard — contract size heterogeneity, which makes the endowment rule decisive — and one distinctive benefit, which is that the exercise manufactures shared accountability among accounts that talk to each other anyway.

In consumer products the economics invert. Twelve users cannot represent millions, recruitment cost per unit of signal is high, and most such questions are answered more cheaply by experiment. Buy-a-feature earns its consumer keep only where experimentation is impossible: before anything exists, across four expensive mutually exclusive directions, or in categories where live testing is ethically or legally constrained. There it runs online with points and is read as structured qualitative evidence.

In platforms and marketplaces the defining feature is the unfunded third party, discussed above. In hardware the denominator stops being engineer-weeks and starts being a mixture of tooling, certification and unit economics, which makes a single price scale dishonest unless it is explicitly converted to money and the conversion is shown. In AI products the list perishes and features are thresholds rather than binaries.

Stage changes the status of the output rather than the method. At an early-stage company, six customers may be a quarter of revenue, so the result is nearly binding and the exercise doubles as retention work — with the well-documented hazard of optimising for the customers you happened to acquire first. At scale, one room cannot carry a roadmap; the output becomes one segment's evidence in an internal argument, and its real function is to break deadlocks between functions arguing from anecdote by producing a fact that neither function controls.
