Example three: Tilhar Instruments, where the method failed

Tilhar Instruments of Coimbatore makes benchtop clinical analysers with a cloud console; roughly 1,900 instruments are installed across diagnostic-laboratory chains. In August 2024 the product team ran a buy-a-feature session with nine laboratory managers, each given ₹100 lakh of play money against a price list of 2,400. The list contained eight items, all software, priced in engineer-weeks. Hardware was excluded on the stated grounds that "hardware is not a feature".

The room funded three items with high ratios: a rebuilt results console at 0.90, laboratory-information-system integration at 0.70, and automated quality-control charting at 0.60. Tilhar built all three, at a cost of about ₹2.7 crore over two quarters, and shipped them in March 2025. Six months later the instrument renewal rate stood at 78 per cent against 78 per cent the year before, and the relationship survey moved from 31 to 33, comfortably inside the noise band for a sample that size.

The post-mortem in October 2025 read forty-one exit interviews from lapsed accounts. The dominant reason for non-renewal, present in twenty-three of them, was a reagent-cartridge misfeed on the TX-200 analyser that caused 6 to 9 per cent of runs to be repeated. That was a hardware revision: new tooling, a supplier requalification and BIS re-certification, together around ₹9 crore and three quarters — more than four times the entire play budget in the room, and therefore unpriceable on a card. It had been excluded from the list because it could not be expressed, and its exclusion was then read by everyone, including Tilhar's own leadership, as evidence that laboratory managers did not care about it. They cared about it more than anything else on the board. They were simply never asked.

The recovery, run in February 2026, inverted the exercise. Stage one was a buy-a-problem session: participants spent a budget across problem statements written as costs to the laboratory — "repeat runs caused by consumable handling", "time spent transcribing results into the LIS", "month-end quality-control paperwork" — with no solution and no engineering price attached, so nothing could be excluded for being unbuildable. Repeat runs took 41 per cent of the room's money. Stage two priced candidate solutions to the top-funded problems only, converting all prices to rupees rather than engineer-weeks so that hardware and software could sit on one board honestly, and setting budgets large enough that the hardware path was reachable by a coalition of seven. Seven of the nine pooled 62 per cent of the combined budget onto the cartridge path.

9. Failure modes, their early warnings, and the cost of catching them late

Pricing by importance. Early sign: the strategically favoured items happen to be the expensive ones, and nobody can name the engineer who estimated them. Diagnostic: have two engineers who have not seen the customer research re-derive prices blind; any item moving by more than a factor of two was priced by opinion. Caught late, the cost is that the whole exercise was circular and the roadmap it justified rests on nothing.

A budget that does not bite. Early sign: a cheerful workshop in which most items are funded and nobody argues. Diagnostic: compute B / P before the session; above 0.5, raise prices or cut budgets. Caught late, the cost is a session that produced a wish list with extra ceremony and two weeks of product time.

Segment mixing at one table. Early sign: almost no coalitions, everyone funding a different item alone. Diagnostic: count items with three or more effective backers; if the number is zero or one, two markets were in one room. Caught late, the cost is a roadmap serving an average customer who does not exist.

Foundational work systematically starved. Early sign: platform and infrastructure cards below a lift of 1.0 in every session you have ever run. Diagnostic: ask whether the item's value is conditional on other items shipping; if yes, the instrument cannot price it. Caught late, the cost is a two-year accumulation of customer-funded features on an architecture nobody paid to maintain — the most expensive failure on this list, and the slowest to become visible.

The exercise read as a commitment. Early sign: a participant emails three weeks later asking when "their" feature ships. Diagnostic: reread the invitation — did it state in writing that this informs prioritisation and is not a delivery commitment? Caught late, the cost is trust, which is the one input to this method that cannot be re-bought.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Is the output evidence or theatre? The measurement school's strongest form is not a complaint about sample size; it is that the instrument has no sampling frame, no randomisation, a facilitator who influences order and framing, and a coalition mechanism that explicitly allows one participant's view to propagate to others — so the output is not a noisy estimate of a population parameter, it is not an estimate of anything. The elicitation school's strongest reply is that this criticism assumes the goal is estimation, when the actual decision is a choice among seven items under time pressure, and the relevant comparison is not with a conjoint study nobody will fund but with the status quo of three internal functions arguing from anecdote. Both positions are coherent. The disagreement would be settled if anyone could show that workshop rankings predict post-launch adoption better or worse than internal judgement — and, remarkably, almost nobody has published that comparison.

Should customers be shown a solution list at all? The discovery school's strongest form: every buy-a-feature session trains customers to think of the product as a menu and trains the team to think of its job as order-taking; the items on the card were invented by the vendor, so the exercise can only ever choose among the vendor's existing imagination, and the most valuable products in any category were not on anyone's list. The counter-argument is that this is an objection to how the output is used rather than to the instrument, and that the two-stage buy-a-problem design absorbs the criticism almost entirely. Those who hold the discovery position most strongly do not accept that reply, on the grounds that stage two reintroduces the menu.

Equal or weighted budgets? One-customer-one-vote treats the exercise as research into a segment and argues that weighting by revenue merely re-encodes the sales pipeline you already knew. One-rupee-one-vote treats it as a resource-allocation exercise for a business that must survive, and argues that pretending a ₹40 lakh account and a ₹4.2 crore account have equal claims on engineering is sentimentality. The position that has the best of the argument in practice is procedural rather than substantive: run both, and report only the items that survive both, as Rukmini did. That is a smaller claim than either camp wants.

Play money or real commitment? A minority school runs the exercise with real consequences — development credits purchased against the next renewal, or a signed letter of intent contingent on delivery. Its strongest argument is that play money is exactly the unconstrained instrument the technique was invented to replace, merely with a smaller number of hypothetical units. The strongest counter is that real money converts the session into a commercial negotiation in which only the well-funded customer speaks, procurement rather than operations attends, and the coalition dynamic — the actual source of insight — disappears entirely, because nobody negotiates in public. Both effects are real and the trade-off has no general resolution.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in four visible ways. They spend more time on the list than on the workshop, because they know that a closed-choice instrument can only ever answer within its menu, and they have at least once seen a session confidently rank seven things while the eighth, unwritten, was the whole problem. They ask about the endowment rule and the job titles before they look at any number, and they report lift and effective backers rather than raw totals, because raw totals invite the reader to believe a measurement occurred. They treat a re-estimate as a reason to re-run rather than to recompute, having learned that demand is a function of price. And they lead the write-up with the refusals, sent to participants within ten working days, because they understand that the technique spends customer goodwill and that only an honest account of what will not be built renews the credit.

The negative tell is equally reliable. Someone who has merely studied the technique presents a ranked bar chart, uses the word "data", compares this quarter's ratios to last quarter's, and cannot say who declined the invitation.

12. What each protagonist decided

Rukmini committed the two quarters to the surgeon mobile schedule — the only item winning under both endowment rules — and to the NABH audit pack, on the grounds that four of six hospitals funded it, that it carried 3.9 effective backers, and that accreditation cycles gave it a natural deadline. She funded ABDM interoperability off the board from a protected platform allocation, stating in writing that it was complementary work the instrument could not price and that its low ratio was an artefact of the method rather than a finding. She wrote to Trilok Hospitals Group explaining why the auto-optimiser was not funded, with Exhibit 2 attached.

Kabir did not build fixed up-front pricing despite it being his consumers' clear first choice. He built the arrival-window guarantee instead, which both sides could live with, and piloted fixed pricing in two categories where variance in job scope was measurably low — pest control and water-purifier servicing — treating the workshop as evidence that the feature was viable only where the supply side's objection did not apply. He declined to build the named-professional card that the supply side had funded most heavily, and said so publicly, because he could not separate its value from its effect on disintermediation. Whether that was the right call remains, at the time of writing, unresolved.

Three questions for discussion.

  1. Rukmini reported only the item that survived both endowment rules. What has she given up by adopting that standard, and in what circumstances would it cause her to discard a genuinely correct finding?
  2. Kabir's consumers and professionals disagreed about fixed pricing. Is the right response to pick a side, to find the categories where the conflict disappears, or to conclude that buy-a-feature was the wrong instrument for a two-sided question? Defend one answer against the strongest form of the other two.
  3. Tilhar's 2024 session was mechanically flawless and produced a ₹2.7 crore mistake. What general property of closed-choice instruments does that failure illustrate, and what would you need to see in a workshop design before you would trust its output on a decision of that size?

13. Going deeper

Exhibit 4 — Related topics, why each matters next, and what it unlocks
TopicWhy it matters next
Value vs effortThe parent idea. Buy-a-feature is a value-effort matrix with the value axis outsourced to customers and the effort axis supplied by engineering, so understanding how effort is estimated tells you exactly how far the funding ratio can be trusted. Unlocks the ability to read any prioritisation output as two separate claims.
RICE scoringThe internal counterpart: reach, impact, confidence and effort, all estimated by the team. Comparing a RICE ranking with a buy-a-feature ranking on the same backlog is the cheapest available test of whether your internal beliefs about customer value are calibrated.
Kano modelNames the category buy-a-feature is structurally blind to. Customers fund performance attributes and must-haves; they almost never fund delighters, because they cannot want what they have not seen. Unlocks the judgement about when not to ask customers at all.
Weighted scoring and WSJFMakes explicit the weights that a buy-a-feature endowment rule leaves implicit. Weighted shortest job first, in particular, formalises the cost-of-delay reasoning that participants apply informally when deciding whether to coalition-fund a large item.
User story mappingThe technique that builds the price list. Mapping exposes the dependency structure that makes complements under-fundable, and it is the practical way to write cards as outcomes rather than as solutions.
Prioritising under constraintsThe general case of which buy-a-feature is one instance — here the constraint is applied to customers rather than to the team. Unlocks reasoning about capacity allocation, protected platform budgets and the sixty-per-cent pre-commitment that mature companies actually run.
Saying noThe skill the exercise creates demand for. A workshop generates a refusal list by construction; the value of the whole method depends on whether the organisation can communicate those refusals to named customers within two weeks and survive the conversation.
